A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, and appendices. The retained material and v2 additions can be reliably matched.

before.justification: Section 7 and Appendix D report original synthetic experiments on margin, connectivity, sampling optimization, and accuracy on small-margin pairs.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original results on non-BT preferences, real preference datasets, and connectivity-estimation stability in Tables 1–3.

M1.justification: The generative and BT learning objectives, rank normalization, and alternating connectivity optimization remain unchanged. The added experiments use the existing BT learner with new data and an additional linear-head configuration.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates finite synthetic contexts and responses. v2 adds HH-RLHF, PKU-SafeRLHF, SHP, and UltraFeedback training data with a common UltraFeedback test set, extending coverage to real language-model preferences. Section 7.5 also introduces a synthetic scenario that violates BT representability.

E2.justification: The original-score versus rank-normalized and uniform versus optimized sampling comparisons are retained. The added experiments compare data conditions using BT; Llama supplies embeddings and Skywork supplies labels, without adding a competing learning method.

E3.justification: New protocols use 10K pairs per real dataset, a linear reward head on frozen Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct embeddings, and a common Skywork-relabeled test set. The non-BT experiment introduces controls preserving comparison mass and the projection target, plus RMSE and probability-MAE evaluation. Appendix D.3 adds connectivity evaluation for general test comparisons; the original Section 7.1 settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 7.5 and Appendix D.4 add a controlled misspecification analysis testing whether BT recovers the same projection target despite altered preference probabilities. Appendix D.2 adds an analysis of connectivity estimates' sensitivity to stochastic optimization. The original margin and connectivity analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions already report standard errors over five seeds for the original experiments. New Table 3 reports ten connectivity estimations per alpha, aggregated across five seeds, with mean, standard deviation, and relative standard deviation. This adds targeted uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in the original experiments' run counts.

E6.justification: Figures 1–4 retain their results, while Tables 1–3 add substantial new findings. At n=131072, Table 1 reports probability MAE of 0.02754 for BT data and 0.06618 for non-BT data. Table 2 reports 82.170% accuracy for UltraFeedback training versus 78.380% for SHP, although SHP has higher connectivity. Table 3 adds estimator-stability results.

T1.justification: The main theorems are retained, but Appendix D.3 adds a general-test-distribution connectivity definition and Proposition D.1 with its eigenvalue proof. Appendix D.4 derives a zero-flow condition and cycle perturbations preserving the BT projection target. v2 also corrects sigmoid and cross-entropy derivative signs around Equation 81.

C1.justification: The abstract and four contribution statements retain the same substantive claims about CPRD, BT representability, KL projection, and margin/connectivity bounds. The new experiments support these existing claims rather than redefine the central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands practical interpretation: Section 7.6 explains dataset rankings through domain mismatch and the margin/connectivity tradeoff; Section 8 discusses conditional-independence diagnostics and difficulties testing them in high dimensions. Appendix D.3 explains linear connectivity as a proxy for richer hypothesis classes, and D.2 qualifies estimator reliability at extreme sampling parameters.

D1.justification: v2 adds model and labeler identifiers, the real-data connectivity calculation, and implementation details for synthetic perturbations. Appendix D.4 specifies randomly oriented three-cycles, at most 20 cycles per context, and validation/test sizes of 2048. Existing synthetic implementation details remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Balcan et al. (2016) on combinatorial comparisons and references supporting UltraFeedback, SHP, PKU-SafeRLHF, Llama, and Skywork. The existing related-work discussion and central novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section ordering are retained. v2 adds experimental and appendix subsections, expands the discussion, and adds acknowledgements. It also changes the displayed author name from Maria-Florina Balcan to Nina Balcan and replaces the preprint footer with conference publication information.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the empirical displays with three new tables covering misspecification, real-dataset comparisons, and estimator stability. Figures 1–4 retain their curves and captions but change plot typography. The overall two-column main text and single-column appendix layout remain.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical grounding of the paper's diagnostic claims. Beyond v1's small synthetic setting, it tests misspecification with a controlled projection target, demonstrates connectivity on real preference data, and quantifies estimator stability. Supporting derivations make these additions assessable. The real-data evidence remains limited to frozen linear heads and one relabeled test distribution, but the combined gains meaningfully strengthen the paper's credibility and practical relevance.
